import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Rational distance problem

*References:*
- [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unit_square#Rational_distance_problem)
- [mathoverflow/418260](https://mathoverflow.net/questions/418260/)
asked by user [Yuan Yang](https://mathoverflow.net/users/177957/yuan-yang)
- D19 in [Unsolved Problems in Number Theory](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-0-387-26677-0)
by *Richard K. Guy*
-/

namespace RationalDistanceProblem

open EuclideanGeometry

def UnitSquareCorners : Fin 4 → ℝ² :=
  ![!₂[0, 0], !₂[1, 0], !₂[1, 1], !₂[0, 1]]

/--
Does there exist a point in the plane at rational distance from all four vertices of the unit square?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11 51]
theorem rational_distance_problem :
    answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ P : ℝ² , ∀ i, ¬ Irrational (dist P (UnitSquareCorners i)) := by
  sorry

end RationalDistanceProblem

reformulations.difference: Expresses rationality of each distance as `¬ Irrational (dist P (UnitSquareCorners i))`, rather than giving an explicit rational witness.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Mathlib defines `Irrational x` as `x ∉ Set.range ((↑) : ℚ → ℝ)`. Thus, classically, `¬ Irrational x ↔ ∃ q : ℚ, (q : ℝ) = x`. Applying this equivalence under the existing `∃ P` and `∀ i` gives exactly the source's condition. The complete existential equivalence was proved in `/workspace/review/scratch.lean`, without using the conjecture or any sorry-dependent result.

sources_consulted: Richard K. Guy, Unsolved Problems in Number Theory, 3rd ed. (2004): https://doi.org/10.1007/978-0-387-26677-0 and https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-0-387-26677-0_5 (metadata and bibliography; D19 full text access-restricted).

T. G. Berry, “Points at rational distance from the corners of a unit square,” Annali della Scuola Normale Superiore di Pisa 17 (1990), 505–529, especially the introduction on pp. 505–506: https://www.numdam.org/item/ASNSP_1990_4_17_4_505_0/ and https://www.numdam.org/item/ASNSP_1990_4_17_4_505_0.pdf
review.notes: Both declarations are faithful. The four distinct corners are correctly enumerated, and `ℝ²` carries the Euclidean L² metric, not the sup metric. Wikipedia and the cited MathOverflow question explicitly allow a point anywhere in the plane; Berry's introduction corroborates this and explicitly references Guy's D19. MathWorld's inside-square wording is a variant, not a restriction imposed by the file's direct online sources. Lean checks passed for the distance formula, corner injectivity, unit side and √2 diagonal, exclusion of every vertex and the centre as trivial solutions, and yes/no answer polarity. The cited online sources still record the problem as open; MathOverflow's counterexample concerns an auxiliary elliptic-curve rank claim. Although Guy's D19 full text was inaccessible, both declarations were independently verified against the explicit cited online statements.
